'Before the donation drive, I want us registered properly,' said Lakshmi, putting a folder on Shreya's desk.
'Good,' said Shreya, a lawyer at the legal aid clinic. 'I'll draft the trust papers with you. And the bank account goes in the trust's name, not yours.'
'And every rupee goes in a ledger the same day?'
'Yes, with a receipt number. A chartered accountant should look at the books once a year.'
'Can donors see the accounts?'
'They should. A short summary on your page each quarter.'
Lakshmi hesitated. 'Won't some people think we're showing off?'
'People give more when they can see where it goes. And clear records help whenever the authorities ask.'
Lakshmi nodded and wrote on the folder: Ledger. Receipts. Quarterly summary.

qa.q: Whose name should the bank account be in?
qa.a: The bank account goes in the trust's name, not Lakshmi's.

qa.q: What worried Lakshmi about sharing the accounts?
qa.a: Lakshmi was worried that some people would think the trust was showing off.

qa.q: What other step could Lakshmi add to keep donors informed?
qa.a: Lakshmi could invite one donor each quarter to look over the ledger in person, since seeing the books first-hand builds trust.

qa.q: How might a donor see the quarterly summary?
qa.a: A donor would likely feel trusted and reassured, and more willing to give again, because they can see where the money goes. 🙂

grounding: Shows an organiser registering a trust with a lawyer's help, keeping clear records and sharing accounts with donors.

passage:
I'm Ramesh, and for the first year the Ward 9 Library ran out of a biscuit tin. People handed me cash at the gate, and I wrote amounts in a school notebook when I remembered.
Then a retired teacher sent a large cheque and asked for a receipt with a registration number. I didn't have one. I felt like a fraud, though I'd never taken a rupee.
My friend Anjali works in a law office, and she introduced me to a lawyer who helped us register a small trust. It took two months of forms. After that, every rupee went into the trust's bank account, every expense had a bill, and the treasurer and I both signed.
Each quarter we sent donors a one-page statement: money in, books bought, rent paid. The retired teacher wrote back, "Now I can tell my friends to give too."

qa.q: Where did the library keep money during its first year?
qa.a: It ran out of a biscuit tin, with amounts written in a school notebook.

qa.q: How did Ramesh feel when asked for a receipt with a registration number?
qa.a: Ramesh felt like a fraud and ashamed, even though no money had ever been taken, because there was nothing official to show.

qa.q: Which other safeguard could the library add as it grows, and why?
qa.a: It could ask an outside accountant to check the books once a year, so donors see an independent view and not only the library's own statement.

qa.q: How does the retired teacher see the library after the quarterly statements start?
qa.a: The teacher trusts it enough to encourage friends to donate, because the money in and out is now visible.

grounding: It shows an organiser who registers a trust with legal help, keeps clear records and shares accounts with donors to protect their trust.

Mentor's note, after the quarterly review with Aditi
When Aditi started the free tuition centre, donations came by phone transfer to her personal account. Last month two donors asked her, gently, where their money had gone. She came to me upset, holding printouts of her bank app, trying to separate tuition money from her own groceries.
Today I saw what she has done since. With help from a lawyer at the legal aid clinic, she has registered the centre as a trust. It has its own bank account. Gurpreet, the volunteer treasurer, keeps a ledger with every bill pasted in beside the entry.
She showed me the one-page summary she will now send donors every quarter.
I suggested she also put the registration number on every receipt. She wrote it down at once.
— Harpal

qa.q: Who keeps the ledger at the tuition centre?
qa.a: Gurpreet, the volunteer treasurer, keeps a ledger with every bill pasted in beside the entry.

qa.q: What was Aditi feeling when she came to her mentor with printouts?
qa.a: She was upset and anxious, because donors had asked where their money went and her own spending was mixed up with the tuition money.

qa.q: What else could Aditi do to keep donors' trust, and why?
qa.a: She could invite donors to visit the centre once a year and see the ledger, so trust rests on what they see as well as on paper.

qa.q: How might Gurpreet see the new system?
qa.a: Gurpreet may feel steadier and more responsible, with a clear ledger and bills that protect the treasurer if anyone asks questions.

grounding: It shows an organiser moving donations into a registered trust with legal help, keeping clear records and planning to share accounts with donors.
